query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Thermal aging of the metastable Mg-containing lightweight HEA promotes a diffusion‐controlled nucleation and growth process that leads to the formation of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. These precipitates disrupt the continuity of the passive oxide scale and serve as microstructural stress concentrators, thereby reducing the alloy’s corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance in service.
generation.material_initial_state: A Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state with a uniform distribution of alloying elements.
generation.intervention: Controlled thermal aging (heat treatment) at temperatures representative of high-temperature service regimes (e.g., 600–800°C) for varying durations.
generation.conditions: A controlled comparison between samples kept in the initial as-cast metastable state (or rapidly quenched to preserve it) and samples subjected to the thermal aging treatment under identical environmental conditions (corrosive/oxidative atmospheres).
generation.structural_mediator: Nucleated Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates that form and subsequently coarsen with aging.
generation.mechanism: Thermal energy drives Mg atoms out of the solid solution, leading to phase separation into Mg-rich intermetallic compounds. The growing precipitates create local inhomogeneities that interrupt the formation and continuity of the protective passive oxide layer. These microstructural discontinuities, along with strain at the precipitate/matrix interfaces, lead to microcracking under thermal stress, thereby undermining the corrosion and oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast (metastable) state, aged samples will exhibit discrete, coarser Mg-rich intermetallic phases. This microstructural evolution will correlate with a measurable degradation in the integrity and effectiveness of the passive oxide film, leading to higher corrosion rates and poorer oxidation resistance under high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: The metastable, homogeneous solid-solution state where alloying elements are uniformly distributed and the protective oxide layer is intact, providing inherent corrosion and oxidation resistance.
generation.boundary: Service regimes above approximately 600°C and prolonged exposure durations, where diffusion is sufficiently accelerated to drive intermetallic precipitation; below these conditions the alloy is expected to retain its beneficial metastable properties.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of Mg-rich intermetallic formation, including the critical time and temperature thresholds, as well as the quantifiable impact of precipitate morphology on passivation breakdown, remain to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set remains in the as-cast (or rapidly quenched) metastable state, and the other set is subjected to controlled thermal aging at 600, 700, and 800°C for a range of durations. Both sets are then exposed to identical corrosive and oxidative test environments. Conduct microstructural analysis and surface examinations to assess the presence and extent of Mg-rich intermetallic formation and the integrity of the passive oxide layer.
measurements: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for phase and microstructure analysis
X-ray diffraction (XRD) and energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) to quantify intermetallic precipitate formation
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to monitor oxide layer composition and continuity
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and potentiodynamic polarization tests to evaluate corrosion resistance
Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) for oxidation resistance performance assessments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged samples fail to show a statistically significant increase in Mg-rich intermetallic phases, or if the passive oxide layer remains as continuous and protective as in the unaged, metastable condition (i.e., no measurable degradation in corrosion and oxidation resistance), then the proposed mechanistic hypothesis will be falsified.
